claims.text: The creep resistance of the FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy coating under sustained stress at high temperature is governed by the formation of a stable nanoscale oxide dispersion.
The nanoscale oxide dispersion acts as a barrier to dislocation movement.
Restricting dislocation movement reduces progressive plastic deformation and creep rate.
The initial material is a polycrystalline FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy with a uniform grain-size distribution.
In situ high-temperature TEM or X-ray diffraction under continuous loading can be used to investigate the proposed oxide-mediated creep mechanism.
The principal structural mediator is a nanoscale oxide dispersion.
Oxide particles pin dislocations and reduce their mobility through oxide-dispersion strengthening.
At 800°C and 200 MPa over 100 hours, the coating is predicted to exhibit a 30% reduction in creep rate relative to the uncoated substrate.
Creep rate will be measured as strain rate on a scale of 10^-4 s^-1.
The proposed mechanism operates between 700°C and 900°C and between 100 MPa and 300 MPa.
The composition and spatial distribution of the oxide dispersion may affect creep resistance.
In situ TEM or X-ray diffraction may fail to capture some microstructural features relevant to creep.
A controlled comparison of otherwise equivalent coatings with and without the nanoscale oxide dispersion can test the hypothesis.
The hypothesis is falsified if the creep rate without the oxide dispersion is not at least twice the creep rate with the oxide dispersion.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome uses an uncoated substrate as its baseline and predicts only a 30% creep-rate reduction, whereas the falsification experiment uses a coating without oxide dispersion as its control and requires at least a twofold rate difference. If these controls were treated as equivalent, the predicted 30% reduction would itself fail the stated factor-of-two criterion.
